meta.description: George Carlin really said it — in the “Dumb Americans” routine of his HBO special Life Is Worth Losing, live from the Beacon Theatre, 5 Nov 2005.

answer.sourceLine: Carlin delivered the line in the “Dumb Americans” routine of his thirteenth HBO special, Life Is Worth Losing, recorded simultaneously with the live broadcast from the Beacon Theatre in New York on 5 November 2005. Wikiquote carries it in its sourced section for that special, and full transcripts of the show contain the passage.

Wikipedia ↗ records that the album was made at the Beacon Theatre in New York on 5 November 2005, recorded simultaneously with the live broadcast of the HBO special, and released on 10 January 2006 through Eardrum Records and Atlantic Records.

author.bio: George Denis Patrick Carlin (1937–2008) was an American comedian, satirist, social critic, actor and author — the man behind “Seven Words You Can Never Say on Television” and a career that ran from clean-cut 1960s television spots to fourteen HBO specials. Life Is Worth Losing, his thirteenth, was one of the darkest: suicide, torture, natural disaster, and a closing stretch on who really runs the country. He died in Santa Monica in June 2008, less than three years after taping it.

misattribution.heading: What usually goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right; almost everything around it is missing or wrong. Carlin is one of the internet’s most faked bylines, so a Carlin line arriving with no source attached is normally a reason to worry — this is the rare case where the words check out and only the paperwork is absent.

items.why: AZQuotes ↗ runs the passage under Carlin’s name with no special, no venue and no year. That is how a documented 2005 stand-up routine ends up circulating as a free-floating internet slogan.

Video clips are nearly always posted under the title “The American Dream.” On the album the routine is listed as “Dumb Americans” — see the track listing on Wikipedia ↗. The popular title is the internet’s, not Carlin’s.

Wikiquote’s Misattributed section for Carlin hands “The Paradox of Our Time” back to Bob Moorehead and lists a run of chain-email pieces he never wrote. This line is not in that section — it is in the sourced one. Wikiquote ↗

Quoted alone it reads as an aphorism. In performance it is one beat of a longer passage — the next sentences are “You and I are not in the big club” and the turn about it being the same club they beat you over the head with. See the full transcript ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Carlin said it on camera on 5 November 2005, in Life Is Worth Losing — it is the sourcing, not the attribution, that keeps going missing. Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗

context.heading: Why this one line outlived the special
lead: The passage sits near the end of a long stretch on what Carlin calls the owners of the country — the people who, in his telling, own the land, the corporations, the media and the politicians, and who want a population just educated enough to run the machines and just dumb enough not to object. The joke is the pivot: after building the case that a small group runs everything, he turns and tells the audience where they stand in it.

Nothing about the delivery is subtle, and that is the point. The line survives as a nine-word summary of an eight-minute argument, which is also why it travels without its source attached: it works as a slogan even when nobody remembers it was a punchline in a 2005 comedy special about death.
context.detailsSummary: What else was in the special
detailsBody: Life Is Worth Losing was recorded at the Beacon Theatre in New York on 5 November 2005 and broadcast live on HBO the same night. During the taping Carlin mentioned that he had been sober for 341 days.

The album version runs 71 minutes and was released on 10 January 2006 by Eardrum Records and Atlantic Records; a DVD followed on 27 February 2007. It was nominated for Best Comedy Album at the 49th Grammy Awards and lost to Lewis Black’s The Carnegie Hall Performance.
context.pull: It works as a slogan even when nobody remembers it was a punchline.
